deep.reconstruction:
Text (lower right).
(1) -11+4i ≡ 1 (mod -1+2i). Write m = -11+4i and M = -1+2i (my labels, suggested by the second line). Then m - 1 = -12+4i = (-1+2i)(4+4i), so the congruence holds.

What the numbers are. N(m) = 121+16 = 137, a rational prime ≡ 1 (mod 4), so m is a Gaussian prime. N(M) = 5, so M is also a Gaussian prime. Both are 'primary' in Gauss's sense of the 1832 memoir: b even and a+b ≡ 1 (mod 4), i.e. each is ≡ 1 (mod 2+2i).

(2) m/M = 3 4/5 + 3 2/5 i (as transcribed). Directly, (-11+4i)/(-1+2i) = (-11+4i)(-1-2i)/5 = (19+18i)/5 = 3 4/5 + 3 3/5 i. The real part agrees with the page. The imaginary part should be 3 3/5, not 3 2/5. This is either a misreading of a small handwritten fraction or a slip by Gauss. The quotient m/M is the point needed to place m relative to the lattice M·Z[i] in the drawing.

Interpretation (mine). By the biquadratic reciprocity law for primary primes, m ≡ 1 (mod M) gives [m/M]_4 = 1. Hence [M/m]_4 = 1, i.e. -1+2i should be a biquadratic residue mod -11+4i.

Direct check (mine). Z[i]/(m) ≅ Z/137, with i ↦ 37, since 4i ≡ 11 and 4^{-1} ≡ 103 (mod 137). Then M ↦ 73, and 73^34 ≡ 1 (mod 137), where 34 = (137-1)/4. So -1+2i is indeed a quartic residue.

Drawing. The grid is roughly 52 px per unit.
- A large tilted square with vertices at about (440,250), (1015,45), (1225,625), (650,830). Its sides are roughly 11+4i and -i(11+4i), so it has side length sqrt(137): a square of the lattice generated by ±11±4i, an associate or conjugate of m. It is presumably a fundamental square for Z[i] mod m, containing N(m) = 137 residue classes.
- Inside it are a second system of tilted lines (an inner square or parallelogram) and diagonals.
- There are rows of lattice points with hatched unit segments marking selected points, in seven rows of 2–4 marks.

The drawing appears to be a geometric lattice-point count of the kind Gauss used in his Nachlass on biquadratic residues. That is, a Gaussian-integer analogue of 'Gauss's lemma' or the Eisenstein-style counting. It would count which multiples of a residue system fall in which quadrant or region, to determine the quartic character of M mod m (or vice versa). The page thus seems to illustrate or test biquadratic reciprocity on the example m = -11+4i, M = -1+2i. The exact counting rule cannot be read off with certainty.
errors: The quotient (-11+4i)/(-1+2i) equals 19/5 + 18/5 i = 3 4/5 + 3 3/5 i. The transcribed imaginary part 3 2/5 is wrong. This is likely a transcription misreading of the small fraction, or else a slip by Gauss.
The precise meaning of the hatched lattice points and the inner lines is not stated on the page; any reading of them as a Gauss-lemma-type count is interpretive.

results.usually_credited_to: Biquadratic reciprocity: stated by Gauss, first published proofs by Jacobi (lectures) and Eisenstein (1844); Gauss's own geometric Nachlass fragments are published in Werke II

deep.surprise_reason: Worked numerical examples and lattice figures for biquadratic residues in Z[i] are known from Gauss's Nachlass (Werke II); this page is one more such example without a new identifiable result.
